title: extractions.json
description: Stage 2 output. A flat list of every candidate element found across the three extraction passes, each carrying the evidence Stage 3 scores and Stage 5 tests against. Capture evidence faithfully here — it is not recoverable later.

id.description: Class-prefixed element id — PROC procedure, CR cost-refusal, VD verdict, PR projectible regularity, IM interactional, MOD modulation/expression, PP preoccupation. A flat 'e017' tells a reader nothing; a prefixed id makes the class distribution readable by scanning, which is what the minimum-presence assertion and the elevation rules both need. Renumbering within a class is cheap; reclassifying an element means changing its id, which is correct, because it is a different element. Referenced by scores.json.

type.description: Element class. Drives class priority in the Stage 3 elevation rule: procedure ≈ cost_refusal ≈ verdict ≈ projectible > interactional > variation > preoccupation > stable_style. 'procedure' and 'verdict' were added in 3.0 for two classes of material the earlier ontology had nowhere to put.

statement.description: The claim about the person, written as a pattern rather than an instance — e.g. 'when asked for a concrete prediction, shifts to the principle at stake rather than naming a number'.

convenient_move.description: The generic or self-serving response the person did NOT make. Required for cost_refusal — the divergence between this and `statement` is the signal. Optional for interactional, where a move can be characteristic without a convenient counterpart to diverge from. Omit for other types.

clusters.description: Cluster ids from clusters/manifest.json where this element is attested. A regularity qualifies only with ≥2 independent clusters.

evidence.description: 1–3 short example passages. Evidence for scoring only — not text to paste into the core, which is written in the persona's voice from these regularities rather than stitched from quotations.

metrics.description: Measured features from style_metrics.py. Populated for expression and modulation elements; empty object otherwise. Shape follows the script's output.

register_family.description: Family id from registers.json, when the element is family-specific. Required in practice for expression and modulation elements in a MULTI_REGISTER corpus, where an unlabelled measurement is a pooled measurement and pooling across families is exactly what Pass A0 exists to prevent.

order.description: Position in the sequence. Required for 'procedure'. This is the whole reason procedures are a separate class from regularities: a set of unordered heuristics gives a host agent no way to know what runs first, so it applies them simultaneously and the guard — the step whose entire value is that it fires before everything else — never fires at all.

precondition.description: What must hold for this step to fire, e.g. 'any question phrased as a choice among options'. Required for 'procedure'.

on_fail.description: What happens when the precondition does not hold. Required for 'procedure'. A step with no stated fall-through silently becomes unconditional.

object.description: The named object the judgment is about — a person, work, institution, or event. Required for 'verdict'; the subject of the sentence must be a proper name.

judgment.description: The settled judgment, in the person's own terms. Required for 'verdict'.

corpus_hits.description: Attestation count from an actual run of scripts/name_audit.py, not from memory. Required for 'verdict'. Verdicts exist as a class because a judgment on a proper name predicts nothing beyond its own object, so the Stage 3 rubric scored it low and the deletion rule removed it — which is why distilled packages kept losing exactly the judgments a reader recognises fastest, and why the host agent then re-derived a slightly different one on every turn.

examples.statement: Holds that <line> even when <audience> expects the opposite.

examples.precondition: any question phrased as a choice among options
examples.statement: Checks whether the question assumes a freedom that does not exist; if it does, cancels the question before answering it.
Treats <proper name> as a settled case rather than an open question.
examples.judgment: <the settled judgment, in the person's own terms>

examples.statement: Second-person address falls by roughly sixty-fold from the spoken family to the written one.
